messages.body_plain:
With the add schemes the output looks basically the same as the drop schemes, but the interpretation is a little different. In this case the sequential scheme p-value is indicating whether "adding a set of equality constraints to item results in an unusually lower-log likelihood change; hence, adding the constraints results in a model the fits significantly worse". For the drop schemes the opposite setup is true since the question is about removing equality constraints rather than adding them. For the drop schemes look at the p-values as "if the equality constrain were removed does the new model have an unusually high log-likelihood compared to the base model?". The interpretation is always relative to whatever base model is being tested, but suffice it to say a small p-value always indicates the presence of some type of DIF. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Best way to evaluate test information (or interpret a & b parameters) for models with 3 or more dimensions
messages.body_plain:
Plots for 3+ dimensions are much more difficult to work with, so you don't really get the nice unidimensional outputs. Plus, the multidimenisonal models are compensatory in nature, so if you have cross-loading you have to interpret all the results as partial coefficients. You can try to get some plots out of the plot() function (see the documentation for what limited support is offered for 3 dimensional models), but overall it's usually better to interpret the coefficients directly. HTH.

Phil

library(mirt)

#single factor
set.seed(12345)
a <- a2 <- matrix(abs(rnorm(15,1,.3)), ncol=1)
d <- d2 <- matrix(rnorm(15,0,.7),ncol=1)
a2[14:15] <- a[14:15] + .5
d2[14:15] <- d[14:15] + c(-.5, .5)
itemtype <- rep('2PL', nrow(a))
N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(a2, d2, N, itemtype, mu = .1, sigma = matrix(1.5))
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- c(rep('D1', N), rep('D2', N))
models <- 'F1 = 1-15'

mirtCluster()

# first five items as anchors
mod_ref <- multipleGroup(dat, models, group = group,
                         invariance=c(colnames(dat)[1:5], 'free_var','free_means'))
out1 <- DIF(mod_ref, c('a1', 'd'), scheme='add', items2test = 6:15, p.adjust = 'BH')
out1$adj_pvals

out2 <- DIF(mod_ref, c('a1', 'd'), scheme='add_sequential', items2test = 6:15, p.adjust = 'BH')
out2$adj_pvals

HTH.

Phil

         Thank you for the reply. Sorry to trouble you with one more question, regarding errors resulting from my most complex dimensional model. For a rating scale (1-5) studying interest in influencing others, I have 8 related subscales (Management, business, marketing, etc) with 4 items each.

I tried to remove any of the 8 subscales from the model to make 7-dimensions and the model converged without errors or warnings. I also tried changing the starting seed but to no avail. I wonder if you have any input on the cause of this---are 8 dimensional models just not possible, or is my script faulty, and is there a workaround?

Thank you so much for your time, I'm trying to craft a dissertation proposal on the application of IRT to interest items, if I get to the next stage I'll be sure to credit you for your help and your super handy mirt package!

Sincerely,
Colin Wee

Mgmt = 1, 2, 3, 4

Mkt = 9, 10, 11, 12

These types of errors occasionally occur due to poor starting values. You may want to try the GenRandomPars input to mirt() to generate a random set of starting values. Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Keri,

These DIF methods are somewhat distinct, but often relate to similar phenomenon. If you're LR approach contains many degrees of freedom due to comparing multiple parameters then you may find the power to detect DIF decreases, which could explain your phenomenon. The LR test really relates better to the NCDRF statistics because both families are looking for differences in the response curves at any θ location, whereas the CDRF statistics are looking for systematic changes across the groups after weight the differences in the response curves by the underlying distribution of theta, g(θ). Could you provide more information about the issue? Then I wouldn't be speculating so much as to what could be happening. Thanks.

Phil

Yes, this sounds like it was a df issue then. There's probably only a few parameters that are difference across the groups, so there are many unnecessary df being used in the LR test (e.g., if the first two intercepts were different only then testing the remaining third, fourth, fifth, ...., only decreases power). You could try isolating different sets of item 7's parameters to determine where the differences are, which is very analogous in the context of ANOVA analyses to run post-hoc tests to determine where the effects lay. In any event, I think this is one of those cases where the DRF statistics are probably outperforming traditional likelihood-based parametric DIF tests.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: SEs for expected test scores
messages.body_plain:
If you're doing this manually then you'll have to obtain some set of parameters drawn from the posterior distribution. Obtaining bootstrap estimates is one approach or using draws assuming a multivariate normal posterior sampling distribution (both can be done via mirt::draw_parameters()). Then you'd have to run expected.test() on every set of parameters obtained, sort each conditional theta location expected score, and obtain the 95% CI from the conditional sorted values. Note that this will give you 95% CI only on conditional theta terms; for the joint confidence interval an alternative approach would be required, which would take an enormous number of samples to obtain accurately. HTH.

Phil

The "after 101 iterations" tells me that the inclusion of the random school intercept effect + combination of the lr fixed effects has caused issues in the sampling scheme. It's hard to say what exactly went wrong without seeing the data first hand, but I suspect this has to do with extreme parameters obtained during the M-step updates. IRT methods can be fragile given the categorical response natures of the data, so sometimes scaling can be problematic, as well as other issues such as slopes tending to ±∞. You could try different starting values to see if you have any luck there, but I can't guarantee this issue can be fixed.

Phil
